records.title: Abacus Platform Purpose and Competition Architecture
records.publicText: Abacus is a full-stack competition-management platform used for the Wisconsin-Dairyland Programming Competition, a high-school programming competition hosted with CSTA Wisconsin-Dairyland and Marquette University ACM. The platform supports school and team registration; teacher, student, administrator, and judge workflows; help requests and communication; point leaderboards; student code submission; automated grading through Judge0; submission review; results management; Blue, Gold, and Eagle Divisions; and virtual and in-person competition workflows. Its architecture includes a React frontend with Vite, TypeScript and JavaScript, a Python backend API with REST-style endpoints, MySQL, Judge0 for compiling submitted code and running test cases, Docker, Docker Compose, WSL Ubuntu, and DBeaver. Mark’s team was initially assigned to TA-Bot / MAAT; after the previous Abacus team was unable to complete the competition platform, their professor asked them to take over Abacus because of their strong progress. The team continued completing MAAT while rebuilding, testing, stabilizing, and delivering Abacus within one semester rather than a traditional two-semester capstone timeline.
records.shortText: Full-stack Wisconsin-Dairyland competition platform with registration, divisions, grading via Judge0, and React/Python/MySQL architecture. Delivered in one semester after Mark’s team also continued MAAT.

records.title: Abacus April 2026 Live Competition Scale and Stability
records.publicText: The April 15, 2026 live competition used Abacus to support approximately 200–300 high-school students, teachers, judges, and administrators during the Wisconsin-Dairyland Programming Competition, a live event lasting approximately three hours. The team improved a platform that had previously struggled with server crashes, lag, system overload, and incomplete competition support. Mark approves the outcome statement that the April 15, 2026 competition ran without major server crashes, platform failures, critical bugs, or major lag. Mark also approves that this was the first completely successful Abacus iteration in recent years, that the team was recognized as the hardest-working senior capstone team, and that the team completed both MAAT and Abacus during one academic year. Mark and his team helped deliver one of the smoothest and most stable recent iterations of the competition platform.
records.shortText: April 15, 2026 live Abacus event supported approximately 200–300 students, teachers, judges, and administrators and ran without major crashes, platform failures, critical bugs, or major lag.

records.title: MAAT Platform Purpose and Evaluation Architecture
records.publicText: TA-Bot, now known as MAAT, is an automated homework-evaluation platform used by Marquette University Computer Science professors and teaching assistants. The platform supports programming-assignment submission, instructor-configured test cases, expected inputs and outputs, automated execution, passed and failed test feedback, grading rubrics, observed errors, score calculation, plagiarism-analysis workflows, and instructor and teaching-assistant grading interfaces. Technologies include React, JavaScript, Node.js, REST APIs, MySQL, Docker, Docker Compose, Git, GitHub, WSL Ubuntu, DBeaver, and AST-based analysis.

records.title: Finch Platform Multiplayer and Real-Time Architecture
records.publicText: Finch Web Controller, originally called BirdFighting / BirdVroomVroom, was a COSC 3810 Software Design and Analysis team project that created a browser-based control platform for BirdBrain Finch 2.0 robots. Architecture and tools included Python, Flask, Flask-SocketIO, React, Vite, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Socket.IO, BirdBrain Finch 2.0, the BirdBrain Python library, BlueBird Connector, Bluetooth robot connectivity, localhost development, python app.py, REST routes, WebSocket-style real-time events, Git, and GitHub. Features included a home screen, single-player and multiplayer modes, room creation, six-character join codes, player identity tracking, lobby ready-up, live player counts, per-player controller screens, keyboard and button input, frontend-to-backend Socket.IO events, Finch motor commands, and the robot communication workflow. Finch is a team coursework project, and the public repository is a fork because the original repository was not owned by Mark.

records.title: Finch Design, Documentation, and Multi-Robot Architecture Contribution
records.publicText: Mark contributed heavily to frontend development. His work included Figma mockups, UI sketches, pixel-art layouts, image and design creation, page layouts, controller-screen layouts, visual direction, implementation planning, installation documentation, class setup materials, project onboarding documentation, React/Vite pages, lobby flow, room-code pages, controller screens, Flask route fixes, backend communication planning, local server setup, localhost testing, hardware/software debugging, Systems Lab hosting preparation, and event-driven command structure. As an advanced assignment constraint, the team was challenged to support three Finch robots while other groups were required to support one. The code-level design included Finch A, Finch B, and Finch C, player-to-robot mappings, dedicated robot IDs, backend player state, and architecture for future simultaneous multi-robot control. Near the end of the course, the professor recognized that complete three-Finch integration was likely unrealistic within the remaining timeline. The team still completed the core browser controller, frontend and backend structure, lobby system, command flow, Figma mockups, documentation, and code-level multi-robot architecture. Do not claim complete production-ready three-robot deployment, fully completed simultaneous three-robot control, that Mark solely architected every component, or that Mark led the entire frontend.

records.title: Space SHMUP Gameplay and Architecture Detail
records.publicText: Space SHMUP is a Galaga-inspired vertical arcade space shooter built in Unity using C#. Gameplay includes player ship movement, rotation feedback, projectile combat, enemy spawning, collision detection, shield mechanics, power-ups, weapon upgrades, scene restart behavior, survival gameplay, and enemy waves. Architecture and programming concepts include Unity 2022.3 LTS, C#, MonoBehaviour, object-oriented programming, inheritance, polymorphism, delegates, events, the singleton pattern, component-based architecture, prefabs, Rigidbody physics, colliders, triggers, serialized fields, arrays, lists, dictionaries, Unity scene management, AnimationCurve, Bézier curves, randomization, parallax scrolling, debugging, and playtesting. The enemy system includes shared enemy base behavior with linear, sine-wave, interpolation, and Bézier-curve movement, plus a roaming boss enemy with layered destructible boss shields. The weapon system uses WeaponFireDelegate, fireEvent, subscriber-based weapon components, blaster and spread-shot projectiles, and data-driven weapon behavior. Supporting systems include weighted enemy spawning, random power-up drops, shield upgrades, reusable screen bounds, recursive damage routing, visual hit feedback, parallax backgrounds, and centralized game-state management.
